review_lens: divergent (8 ideation lenses: inversion, constraint-removal, audience-shift, combination, simplification, 10x, expert-lens, open-standards)
pr_title: feat(microservices): flat layout substrate + 17 µservice audit-grade packs (1,515 artifacts)
verdict_rationale: The PR is structurally coherent and the ADRs are well-argued, but several decisions exhibit reasoning patterns common to monoculture risk and hyperscaler-mimicry without independent first-principles validation. The divergent lens surfaces enough 12-month-regret scenarios that I recommend approval with a binding follow-up IP to validate the 3-5 most consequential hidden assumptions BEFORE M02 promotion. Block-grade objections (CRDT monoculture, Annex III binary gate, OpenBao governance fragility) are mitigable via successor ADRs; not blocking PR #143 itself.

stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: Every cited hyperscaler (Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure Foundry, Anthropic Console, Palantir AIP, LangSmith) ships ONE product surface with internal BCs.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if the hyperscaler shape ADR-0136 cites is the PRODUCT MARKETING surface, not the internal service topology? AWS Bedrock the API is one surface; internally Bedrock-runtime, Bedrock-agents, Bedrock-knowledge-bases, Bedrock-guardrails are operated by SEPARATE service teams with separate on-call rotations, separate deployment pipelines, separate AWS SDK clients (`bedrock`, `bedrock-runtime`, `bedrock-agent`, `bedrock-agent-runtime`). The ADR conflates product perimeter with service perimeter. The 6-way split may actually mirror the AWS internal reality more faithfully than the consolidation.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: If migration cost were zero, would we choose 1 µservice or 6? The ADR's strongest cons against the 6-way split are coordination + duplication, both of which are tooling-addressable (per-BC subchart auto-generation). The case for consolidation thins considerably once tooling cost is removed from the comparison.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale (e.g., 1,000 foundry deploys/day) the single-µservice shape has a NOISY-NEIGHBOR risk: a guardrails hotpatch ships behind an eval-only feature, and any incident in eval blocks the runtime release train. AWS internally splits Bedrock-runtime from Bedrock-agent precisely to avoid this.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: An AWS Bar Raiser would push back on the line 'every benchmark ships ONE product perimeter; oyatie's prior split forced consumers and operators to reason about six perimeters.' Bar Raisers care about INTERNAL operability — they would ask: 'Show me the on-call rotation for foundry-guardrails vs foundry-runtime. If it's the same person, you have an org problem not an architecture problem; if it's different people, you've just merged their incident perimeter at the wrong layer.'
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: Foundry traffic grows 50x. Guardrails (CPU-bound regex/classifier) and providers (network-bound LLM round-trips) need orthogonal scaling profiles. The single-µservice Helm umbrella forces them onto coupled deploy cadence. We undo the consolidation in M07 at 5× the cost of preserving the split now. The bc-sources archive becomes the evidence we used to argue WITH ourselves in 6 months.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: End-user gets ONE product surface either way (the public API). The 6→1 saves coordination cost FOR OYATIE, not for the user. This is a developer-experience optimization sold as a hyperscaler-shape match.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: the bc-sources/ archive. 493 files preserved verbatim under bc-sources/<bc>/ is a 'we'll deal with it later' compromise that bloats the foundry tree to 493 files in one directory. Search-and-discovery worsens; doc coherence requires the new BLOCKER lane (foundry-bc-source-coherence) which itself becomes a maintenance tax.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Stripe (per-surface µservices): worse — Stripe ships /v1/charges, /v1/customers as separate teams. vs Palantir AIP (one product): same. vs Anthropic Console (one product): same. Differentiation is zero; we look like Anthropic's API surface, but Anthropic has ONE LLM behind it; we have 6 distinct execution contexts.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve, BUT author successor ADR-0139 within 30 days: 'Foundry per-BC subchart cadence + per-BC release pointer (release/foundry-<bc>/<env>).' This recovers per-BC deploy independence without re-splitting the µservice. The ADR-0136 'Per-BC Helm subchart' bullet is hand-wave language; needs concrete release-pointer design.

stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: Independent scaling dimensions + per-concern SLO targets + per-concern compliance overlays force unbundling.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if mail + calendar + messenger SHARE more substrate than the ADR admits? All three are stateful, all three are personal-context, all three have CalDAV/CardDAV/JMAP/IMAP-class wire protocols, all three need the same identity-and-presence kernel, all three share the same legal-hold and eDiscovery surface. Splitting them into 3 µservices means we author 3 × legal-hold, 3 × eDiscovery, 3 × identity-binding, 3 × presence — the substrate duplication is bigger than the scaling-dimension difference.
divergent_critique.audience_shift: If the audience is enterprise IT (Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace customers), they buy ONE product, one SKU, one SLA, one support contract. The 8-µservice split is internally-justified and externally-invisible — except that the brand-layer 'Connect' survives only in marketing. We've shipped Conway's-Law architecture and called it product strategy.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale: 8 µservices × 11 packs × 13 layers × 6 BCs = 6,864 governance lane runs per CI pass. The flat-and-many topology is CI-cost-quadratic. The Big-Three (Microsoft / Google / Atlassian) own their SLO surface by team, NOT by µservice — they have hundreds of µservices per product but ONE SLO board per product.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: A Google Eng Review Committee would flag 'shorts' (short-form video) being a µservice in the SAME tier as 'notes' (markdown text). These are wildly different operational beasts. Shorts needs GPU-pool affinity, CDN egress budgets, transcode-farm autoscale; notes is CRDT + Postgres. Treating them as peers in a flat topology hides 10x cost asymmetry. Google internally would put shorts under a YouTube-class infra team, not a Workspace-peer team.
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: Mail + Calendar + Messenger need shared substrate (identity, presence, legal-hold, eDiscovery, contact-graph). At 12 months we author 'oya-personal-substrate' as a hidden 9th µservice that the 3 import via Workflow events — which is exactly what the original Connect was, minus the marketing wrapper. We discover that ADR-0132's 'no suites' rule needed a 'no anti-suites' clause.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: Enterprise admin opens Oyatie Workspace admin console. With 8 µservices they configure SSO 8 times? Retention policy 8 times? Legal hold 8 times? If 'no' (because there's a shared admin layer), then the shared admin layer IS the missing 9th µservice. If 'yes', the user experience is worse than Google Workspace.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: shorts. Authoring a from-scratch short-form-video µservice is a 6-12 engineer-month commitment, not a scaffold. The 97-file shorts/ tree is a placeholder; the actual GPU-pool + CDN + transcode-farm operational substrate is not in scope. Same for meet (video conferencing) — the 17 µservices include 2 surfaces that are infrastructurally on par with full hyperscaler products.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Microsoft 365 (one suite, one admin): worse. vs Google Workspace (one suite, one admin): worse. vs Notion (one product, multiple surfaces): worse. vs Atlassian (per-product but bundled admin): same.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve ADR-0135 as-is BUT require a 'shared admin substrate' ADR within 90 days: identity-binding, retention-policy, legal-hold, eDiscovery must live in a shared substrate µservice (candidate name: 'governance-personal' or 'workspace-admin'). Otherwise we re-implement these 8 times and drift.

stress_test_per_decision.decision: Loro 1.x as universal CRDT across 6 µservices
stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: Implicit: one CRDT library across docs/sheets/slides/sites/notes (and possibly forms).

divergent_critique.inversion: What if Loro is the WRONG CRDT for half of these? Loro optimizes for text + tree CRDTs (Yata-like). Sheets is a 2D-array CRDT with formula dependency graphs — Loro doesn't have a first-class sheet primitive; we'd build on top of its map+list. Google Sheets uses a custom CRDT, NOT a general-purpose library; Quip used a custom CRDT; Notion shipped without CRDTs for years. The 'universal CRDT' choice is a generalization that costs sheet-specific optimizations.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: If we could choose any CRDT today: Yjs has the largest ecosystem (10x npm downloads vs Loro), Automerge has the strongest CRDT theory pedigree (Martin Kleppmann + Ink&Switch), Loro is Rust-native and fast but has the smallest community. We optimized for Rust integration; in 12 months when our Workspace surfaces ship in TypeScript via SDK, the Yjs ecosystem advantage compounds.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale with 100M concurrent edits/day: Loro 1.x has not been battle-tested at hyperscaler load. Yjs has Notion (10M+ users), Liveblocks, Tldraw production deployments. Automerge has Microsoft + Ink&Switch. Loro has … itself + early adopters. Operational maturity risk is a real cost.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: A Palantir ontology architect would say: 'You're conflating two different layers. CRDT is for application-state convergence (what's on screen); ontology is for object-state authority (what's true). Loro for application state is fine; you need a separate authority layer for ontology that's strongly consistent, not eventually consistent.' If the ADR doesn't make this distinction, sheets-as-source-of-truth will have ontology drift.
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: Loro 1.x roadmap pivots (commercial license change, primary maintainer leaves, security CVE we can't patch fast because the team is small). We discover that '6 µservices depend on Loro' is a bus-factor-1 dependency. Migration cost: write 6 × dual-CRDT adapter + 6 × backfill replay + 6 × invariant tests. Cost estimate: 12-18 engineer-months. Mitigation we didn't ship: pluggable CRDT trait in oya-shared-crdt-kernel.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: User cares about: no merge conflicts, fast typing, offline editing. Any of Yjs/Automerge/Loro delivers this. Choice of library is invisible to user; the cost of the choice is invisible until the library's governance changes.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: sheets formula reactivity on top of Loro's map+list primitives. This is a research project, not a 'wire up Loro' integration. The 100-file sheets/ tree assumes this is solved.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Google Sheets (custom CRDT): we're a tier behind. vs Quip (custom CRDT): tier behind. vs Notion (no CRDT, last-write-wins): we're ahead. vs Tldraw / Liveblocks (Yjs): community ecosystem behind.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: BLOCK on Loro lock-in. Require: (a) oya-shared-crdt-kernel port trait abstracting Loro behind an interface; (b) one alternate adapter (Yjs or Automerge) compiled in CI even if not deployed; (c) bus-factor SLA — if Loro maintainers <3 active contributors for 6 months, trigger pluggable-CRDT migration ADR. This is a 1-week effort now vs 12-month effort in regret scenario.

stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: User directive 2026-05-17; LTS version pin 2.x; canonical `${openbao:secret/<path>}` SecretReference.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if OpenBao is the WRONG choice because it's a fork? HashiCorp Vault's BUSL license change in 2023 spawned OpenBao via the OpenTofu/Vault community. OpenBao is governed by the Linux Foundation, which is positive, but it inherits Vault's API and operational complexity — a 10-year-old API surface designed for a different era of secret management. AWS Secrets Manager + KMS, GCP Secret Manager + Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault — all are managed, cloud-native, and have post-Vault-era APIs.
divergent_critique.audience_shift: If we're hyperscaler-grade, we operate ON hyperscalers, which means we COULD use cloud-native secret managers and get HSM-backing + IAM-integration + audit-logs for free. Self-hosting OpenBao means we own the operational substrate of the most-sensitive system in the platform. The on-call burden of a self-hosted OpenBao cluster is non-trivial; AWS Secrets Manager has ~5 9s without on-call.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale: OpenBao cluster scaling (Raft consensus, seal/unseal ceremonies, performance under high QPS) is documented but battle-test data is sparse compared to Vault Enterprise (which has Stripe-class deployments). We are committing the platform to a fork with less production telemetry than its source.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: An Anthropic safety team would ask: 'Where does the OpenBao root key live, and who has access?' If the answer is 'in HSM per cell per ADR-0043', that's good — but the per-cell HSM substrate (KMS / CloudHSM / Azure Key Vault HSM) is doing most of the security work. OpenBao is just the access-control layer in front of HSMs we'd need anyway. We could collapse OpenBao + HSM into a single hyperscaler-native abstraction.
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: OpenBao governance fragments (LF foundation reorg, IBM acquires the maintainer team, license re-changes). We're locked into a vault dialect that no managed cloud service speaks. Migration to AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager requires rewriting every `${openbao:secret/<path>}` reference — our canonical SecretReference path is the lock-in.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: User (operator) cares about: secret rotation, audit log, blast radius. OpenBao delivers; cloud-native services also deliver, with less ops burden. End user gets identical UX.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: per-cell OpenBao HA + seal-unseal automation + key rotation under 11 jurisdictional packs. KR-FSS may require KR-domiciled HSM; this is an HSM problem, not an OpenBao problem. The HSM is the load-bearing primitive; OpenBao is a thin access layer.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Stripe (self-hosted Vault Enterprise): same shape, less battle-tested. vs Anthropic (AWS Secrets Manager): worse (less managed). vs Palantir (custom + HSM): same shape, less mature.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve OpenBao for M01-M02, but require: (a) abstract SecretReference behind oya-shared-secret-kernel port trait; (b) alternate adapter for AWS Secrets Manager + GCP Secret Manager + Azure Key Vault; (c) NEVER let `${openbao:secret/...}` appear in business logic — only `${secret:...}` with the resolver chosen per-cell. The user directive said 'OpenBao'; the architecture should say 'pluggable secret manager with OpenBao as default'.

stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: 4 Cedar v4.2 LTS policy fragments per µservice; default-deny + defence-in-depth FORBID.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if OPA + Rego is structurally better for our case? OPA has CNCF graduated status, Kubernetes admission-controller battle-testing, Gatekeeper integration, far larger policy-author community. Cedar has AWS pedigree + formal verification (SMT-backed) but a smaller ecosystem. The verification advantage matters for ABAC over IAM; less so for the kind of multi-tenant data-plane policies we ship.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: If we could choose: Cedar is best for IAM-shaped authz with strong type schemas; OPA is best for arbitrary policy with JSON/YAML inputs; in-house DSL is best when we have a strong type system already (Rust). We chose Cedar without authoring the in-house alternative; the comparison in ADRs is shallow.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale: Cedar policy evaluation per request adds latency. AWS Verified Permissions caches Cedar evals; we'd need to ship a similar caching layer. OPA has battle-tested caching (in-process). Cedar requires the policy-store + entity-store — we ship per-cell, which is OK, but the operational substrate is non-trivial.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: A Palantir ontology architect: 'Cedar's entity model assumes a known entity graph; your ontology IS the entity graph. If you can express ontology types as Cedar entities, Cedar is excellent. If your ontology types are dynamic (user-authored), Cedar's schema-bound model fights you.' This is a real question the ADRs don't address.
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: Cedar's schema-bound model fights against the ontology's dynamic-type runtime. We ship 4 Cedar fragments per µservice × 17 µservices = 68 fragments, then discover we need a 5th fragment for ontology-runtime types. Cedar's static schema means every new ontology Object Type requires a Cedar fragment regenerate. We invent a Cedar-fragment-codegen-from-ontology tool, which is the worst of both worlds.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: End user gets default-deny authz either way. Operator gets policy review surface — OPA's Rego is more readable to security teams than Cedar in 2026 (community familiarity).
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: aligning Cedar entity-model with ontology runtime types. Open question; ADR-0136 doesn't address.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Stripe (in-house authz): different, ours is more open. vs Palantir (in-house): different. vs AWS Bedrock (Cedar): same. vs Google (in-house Zanzibar-like): different, ours less battle-tested.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve Cedar BUT require: (a) authz port trait abstracting Cedar; (b) Rego adapter authored as proof-of-portability (compiled in CI); (c) explicit ADR on Cedar-fragment-codegen-from-ontology pattern OR a Zanzibar-style relationship-based authz overlay for ontology-dynamic types.

stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: Per-pack overlay per µservice; KR is pack #1; canonical-base neutrality CI-enforced.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if 'pack' is the wrong unit and we should use jurisdiction-tagged feature flags instead? A single 'data-residency: KR' tenant flag + a single 'retention-floor: 5y' tenant flag + a single 'audit-seal: required' tenant flag composes more flexibly than 11 × 17 = 187 pack overlay files. The pack model assumes packs are coarse-grained; feature flags assume packs are compositions of fine-grained constraints.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: If we had a perfect compliance-as-code system: AWS Config + Open Policy Agent + a constraint registry like Conftest could express jurisdiction-bound constraints as policies, not as overlays. Overlays are inheritance; constraints are composition. Composition scales better with N jurisdictions.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale: 11 packs × 17 µservices = 187 overlay files now. Add the next 11 jurisdictions (Mexico, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Philippines, Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Turkey, Israel, Argentina) = 374 overlay files. Each new jurisdiction is O(17) author-cost. Composition model: each new jurisdiction is O(1) constraint additions, fan-out is automatic.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: A Stripe compliance architect: 'You picked the inheritance model. Stripe started there too. We moved to constraint composition because EU vs UK vs Switzerland have 80% overlap with 20% delta — the overlay model duplicates the 80%; the constraint model expresses only the delta.'
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: EU → EU-DE → EU-DE-banking → EU-DE-banking-BAIT → … the pack tree grows deeply. KR → KR-FSS → KR-FSS-Tier1-bank → … same. We discover that packs need sub-packs need sub-sub-packs, and the inheritance chain is 4 levels deep. We migrate to constraint composition at the 4-level depth at huge cost.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: Compliance officer (operator) cares about: 'show me how this tenant satisfies KR-FSS clause 12.3'. Inheritance model = navigate pack files. Constraint model = query the constraint store for clause 12.3 satisfiers. Constraint model wins for audit clarity.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: 11 packs authored upfront. Pack-kr is partly populated; the other 10 are likely scaffold-only at 3,686 file count. The 'per-pack' enforcement is a placeholder for content yet to be written.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs AWS GovCloud / China Cloud (separate cloud envs): different shape; ours is multi-tenant. vs Stripe (constraint composition): worse, we picked the model they moved away from. vs Salesforce (pack-per-jurisdiction): same shape, mature there.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve packs as M01 starting shape BUT require successor ADR within 6 months evaluating constraint-composition migration. Specifically: author oya-compliance-constraint-kernel as a parallel surface; express pack-kr both as overlay AND as constraint set; measure author-cost delta. If constraint set wins, migrate.

stress_test_per_decision.decision: Workflow + Ontology as adapter layer (universal inter-µservice)
stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: All inter-µservice flows through Workflow (orchestration) + Ontology (info); products never call each other directly.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if this is THE bottleneck? Every inter-µservice call going through Workflow + Ontology means Workflow's SLO is the SLO ceiling for every cross-µservice interaction. If Workflow has p99 of 50ms, every cross-µservice call inherits >=50ms p99. Synchronous reads (mail reads calendar invite) at 50ms ceiling is fine; high-fanout reads (feed reads 100 users' state) is catastrophic.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: Stripe has direct service-to-service mTLS gRPC with shared schemas (Sorbet). Google has the same (Stubby + protobuf). Both have a service mesh, not an orchestration layer, as the canonical inter-service primitive. Workflow as middleware is a Palantir / SAP convention, not a hyperscaler one. We picked an enterprise pattern and called it hyperscaler.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale: Workflow becomes the central failure perimeter. If Workflow has an outage, every cross-µservice flow stops. The blast radius is the platform. Hyperscalers explicitly avoid this by having the service mesh be the cross-µservice primitive (no orchestrator in the data path).
divergent_critique.expert_lens: A Google SRE: 'You have a service mesh decision pending. Service-to-service should be Istio + mTLS + protobuf. Workflow should be an EVENT topology (Kafka-like) for choreography, not orchestration in the data path. If Workflow is in the data path, you're shipping ESB 2.0.'
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: Cross-µservice latency budgets become Workflow-bound. We discover that 80% of cross-µservice calls don't need orchestration — they're simple reads. We carve out a 'direct read' lane that bypasses Workflow for read-only ontology queries. This is the architecture we should have shipped Day 1.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: User sees latency. Workflow in path = +20-50ms per cross-service call. End-user-perceived latency is the constraint.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: Workflow's own SLO. Workflow is one µservice; if it's the bus for 17 µservices' cross-traffic, its SLO and capacity are the platform's SLO and capacity.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Stripe (mTLS + Sorbet schemas): worse (more latency). vs Google (Stubby + protobuf): worse. vs Palantir (ontology-mediated): same. vs SAP (orchestrator-mediated): same (which is bad company).
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve Workflow + Ontology as the WRITE/MUTATION adapter layer BUT carve out an explicit 'direct read' lane for ontology object queries that bypasses Workflow. Successor ADR within 60 days: 'Cross-µservice read path — ontology direct vs Workflow-mediated'.

stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: Every µservice = canonical global base + localization overlay; ADR-0064 neutrality CI-enforced.

divergent_critique.inversion: What did we canonicalize that should stay per-service? Threat models. The PR ships a threat-model template per µservice — but threat models are deeply per-service (mail's threat model is dominated by SMTP injection + DKIM bypass; messenger's is dominated by MLS key compromise; shorts' is dominated by content moderation evasion). Canonicalizing the FORMAT is OK; canonicalizing the CONTENT erases the per-service security reasoning. Verify that the 70-artifact-per-µservice template doesn't tempt agents to ship boilerplate threat models that look complete but encode no service-specific reasoning.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: What stayed per-service that should be canonical? Cost-budget templates. Every µservice has a cost-budget file; the FORMAT should be canonical (FinOps Foundation taxonomy: workload-cost, storage-cost, egress-cost). If 17 cost-budget files have 17 different schemas, aggregation is impossible.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale of µservices (170 services): canonical base becomes load-bearing. If canonical base changes (template v2), every service must regenerate. Without a regen tool, drift is inevitable.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: An AWS Bar Raiser: 'Show me the diff between any two µservices' PRDs that's NOT in the per-service-content section. If the diff is large, the template isn't truly canonical; if zero, the template encodes the right boilerplate floor.'
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: Threat models are 17 × copy-paste of the template with placeholder content. We discover during a real security review that no µservice has a threat model worth reading. We re-do all 17 by hand. The template was an audit-grade artifact, not a security artifact.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: Internal user (engineer/security): wants useful artifacts. Canonical-base + per-service content is the right shape IF the per-service content gets authored. The PR ships scaffolds; content authorship is downstream work.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: content authorship. 1,515 artifacts ship as scaffolds; the actual content is the work.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Stripe (templated PRDs): same. vs Palantir (heavy templates): same. vs Anthropic (light templates): different (lighter).
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve canonical-base shape BUT require an 'artifact-quality' lane that measures content-density (non-placeholder content per artifact). If artifacts are >50% placeholder text, the gate fails. Otherwise we ship 1,515 scaffolds and call it 'audit-grade'.

stress_test_per_decision.decision: EU AI Act Annex III gating (binary: yes/no)
stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: Every T2-auto capability flagged for Annex III.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if the binary gate is wrong shape? EU AI Act has 4 risk tiers (unacceptable, high, limited, minimal). 'Annex III: yes' collapses high-risk to a single bucket; 'no' collapses everything else. A graduated tier model lets per-capability authorization scale with risk.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: If we had time to do it right: model risk as a continuum, not a binary. Author capabilities with risk-tier metadata (impact-on-rights, scale-of-deployment, opt-in-vs-opt-out, reversibility). The gate evaluates the metadata, not a frontmatter flag.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale (1,000 capabilities): binary gate over-flags (false-positive admission denials) or under-flags (false-negative compliance breaches). Either failure mode is unacceptable at hyperscaler scale.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: An Anthropic safety team: 'Binary gates are for binary properties. AI risk is not binary. The gate as designed will create either compliance theater (everyone marks Annex III: no) or admission paralysis (everyone marks Annex III: yes, gate blocks). Neither is the goal.'
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: EU AI Act enforcement begins. Auditors ask 'show me your risk classification for capability X'. Our answer: 'Annex III: yes/no boolean'. Auditor: 'That's not a risk classification, that's a coverage flag. Where's the impact assessment, the deployment scope, the reversibility analysis?' We retrofit per-capability risk metadata in M07.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: Affected user (data subject): cares about being protected by graduated risk controls. Binary gate is a step toward this but not the destination.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: defining the risk-tier metadata schema. Easier than retrofitting after enforcement.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs Stripe (limited AI surface, less Annex III exposure): different. vs Anthropic (Claude API as high-risk capability): they have explicit risk-tier reasoning. vs Palantir (FedRAMP + AI risk): they have graduated controls.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve binary gate as M01 starting point BUT require successor ADR within 90 days: 'Graduated AI risk tier classification'. Schema: impact-on-rights (low/med/high/critical), deployment-scope (single-tenant/cell-scoped/region-scoped/global), reversibility (immediate/24h/7d/non-reversible), opt-model (opt-in/opt-out/no-choice). Gate evaluates the tuple, not the boolean.

stress_test_per_decision.stated_rationale: 70 artifacts per µservice × 17 µservices + 11 packs = audit-grade.

divergent_critique.inversion: What if 3,665 files is the WRONG level of granularity and they should be generated from a smaller spec set? If we had a canonical spec per µservice (one JSON document per service with structured fields), we could code-generate PRD.md, threat-model.md, dpia.md, slos/*.yaml, contracts/*.yaml, runbooks/*.md from the spec. The repo would have 17 spec files instead of 3,665 artifact files. Updates to the canonical base regenerate everything.
divergent_critique.constraint_removal: If we had a code-generation pipeline: the spec is the source of truth; artifacts are derived. Drift becomes impossible. Aggregation becomes free.
divergent_critique.ten_x: At 10x scale (170 µservices): 36,650 artifact files. CI scans become slow; ripgrep becomes slow; navigation becomes hostile. Generated artifacts scale; hand-authored don't.
divergent_critique.expert_lens: A Palantir ontology architect: 'You have an ontology product. Why isn't the artifact set itself ontology-defined? Each µservice is an instance of an `OntologyMicroservice` type with fields like prd_text, threat_model, slos[]. Render the artifacts FROM the ontology. You'd be eating your own dogfood.'
divergent_critique.twelve_month_regret_scenario: We accumulate drift. PRD.md says one thing, threat-model.md says another, slos/*.yaml says a third. The 'truth' is unrecoverable. We invent a code-generation pipeline at M07 and regenerate everything from the spec we should have authored Day 1.

stress_test_per_decision.user_value_test: Internal reader (engineer/auditor): hand-authored artifacts feel authoritative; generated artifacts feel disposable. There's a perception cost to generation. BUT — hand-authored artifacts that drift are worse than generated ones that don't.
stress_test_per_decision.feasibility_test: Hardest part: the code-gen pipeline itself. Building it post-hoc is harder than building it Day 1.
stress_test_per_decision.differentiation_test: vs AWS internal (smithy IDL → service docs): they generate. vs Google (BUILD files + design docs as source): mixed. vs Anthropic (spec-driven): aligned. vs Stripe (Sorbet → SDKs): aligned.
stress_test_per_decision.recommendation: Approve current 3,665-artifact shape as M01 reality BUT require: by M03, every µservice has a canonical spec file (one JSON document); by M05, 50% of artifacts are generated from spec; by M07, 90%. Hand-authored content lives in spec; rendered artifacts are derived. This is the only way the artifact set scales to 170 µservices.

twelve_month_regrets.regret_scenario: Loro 1.x roadmap pivots (commercial license change, primary maintainer leaves, security CVE we can't patch fast). 6 µservices depend on Loro — bus-factor-1 dependency. Migration cost: 12-18 engineer-months.
twelve_month_regrets.probability_estimate: 20-30% over 12 months (CRDT library governance is volatile)
twelve_month_regrets.mitigation: Author oya-shared-crdt-kernel port trait NOW; ship one alternate adapter (Yjs or Automerge) compiled in CI. 1-week effort.

twelve_month_regrets.decision: Workflow + Ontology as universal cross-µservice adapter (read path)
twelve_month_regrets.regret_scenario: Workflow becomes the latency ceiling and failure perimeter for all cross-µservice traffic. We carve out a 'direct read' bypass lane in M07 — architecture we should have shipped Day 1.
twelve_month_regrets.probability_estimate: 70% over 12 months (this regret is almost certain at scale)
twelve_month_regrets.mitigation: Successor ADR within 60 days defining read-path vs write-path: ontology direct reads OK; mutations go through Workflow.

twelve_month_regrets.regret_scenario: Guardrails and providers need orthogonal scaling profiles at 50x traffic. Helm umbrella forces coupled deploy cadence. We undo the consolidation at 5× cost.
twelve_month_regrets.mitigation: Author successor ADR-0139: per-BC subchart cadence + per-BC release pointer (release/foundry-<bc>/<env>). Recovers per-BC deploy independence without re-splitting.

twelve_month_regrets.regret_scenario: OpenBao governance fragments. Migration to cloud-native secret managers requires rewriting every `${openbao:secret/<path>}` reference — our canonical SecretReference path is the lock-in.
twelve_month_regrets.probability_estimate: 15-25% over 12 months (LF foundation is stable but small forks are volatile)
twelve_month_regrets.mitigation: Abstract SecretReference behind oya-shared-secret-kernel port trait; use `${secret:...}` in business logic with per-cell resolver.

twelve_month_regrets.regret_scenario: Pack tree grows 4 levels deep (EU → EU-DE → EU-DE-banking → EU-DE-banking-BAIT). Inheritance model duplicates 80% of overlap. Migrate to constraint composition at M07 at huge cost.
twelve_month_regrets.mitigation: Successor ADR within 6 months evaluating constraint-composition. Author oya-compliance-constraint-kernel as parallel surface; measure author-cost delta.

hidden_assumptions.assumption: Hyperscaler product-surface shape (one product perimeter) maps to hyperscaler service-team shape (one service team)
hidden_assumptions.evidence_against: AWS Bedrock externally is one API; internally bedrock-runtime, bedrock-agent, bedrock-agent-runtime, bedrock-knowledge-bases are separate SDK clients with separate service teams. The ADR conflates product perimeter (marketing) with service perimeter (operations).
hidden_assumptions.validation_strategy: Survey 3 ex-AWS / ex-Google / ex-Anthropic engineers on the internal service-team topology of their reference platforms. Confirm whether the cited 'one product' shape is product-marketing or service-engineering.
hidden_assumptions.risk_if_wrong: Foundry consolidation (ADR-0136) is justified by a hyperscaler shape that doesn't exist internally. We've copied the marketing diagram and called it architecture.

hidden_assumptions.assumption: Workflow + Ontology adapter layer can carry ALL inter-µservice traffic (including reads) without becoming the platform's SLO ceiling
hidden_assumptions.evidence_against: Hyperscalers explicitly avoid putting orchestration in the data path. Service mesh (Istio + mTLS + protobuf) is the canonical primitive for synchronous inter-service traffic; orchestration is for choreographed workflows.
hidden_assumptions.validation_strategy: Load-test a representative high-fanout read pattern (e.g., feed assembly reading 100 users' state) through Workflow vs direct ontology read. Measure p99 latency delta and Workflow saturation.
hidden_assumptions.risk_if_wrong: Cross-µservice read SLO is Workflow-bound. Feed assembly, sheet recalc, calendar invite reads all inherit Workflow's p99. End-user latency budget is consumed by the adapter.

hidden_assumptions.assumption: 1,515 audit-grade artifacts have meaningful content density (not placeholder)
hidden_assumptions.evidence_against: PR description claims 'audit-grade' but doesn't measure content-density per artifact. 70 artifacts/µservice is a lot of writing; the per-pack overlay multiplier compounds the volume. Past patterns in this repo (per memory feedback_pr82_dishonest_exit_gate) show willingness to ship scaffolds and call them complete.
hidden_assumptions.validation_strategy: Sample 20 artifacts at random (e.g., microservices/shorts/threat-model.md, microservices/notes/dpia.md, microservices/calendar/runbooks/incident-response.md). Measure: (a) non-placeholder character count; (b) cite-density (references to actual code/specs); (c) auditor-readability (can a security auditor extract a finding from this?).
hidden_assumptions.risk_if_wrong: 1,515 'audit-grade' artifacts are 1,515 scaffolds. The 'audit-grade' claim collapses on first external audit. Re-authoring is M07 work at significant cost.

hidden_assumptions.assumption: 11 jurisdictional packs cover the regulatory fan-out we'll face in 12 months
hidden_assumptions.evidence_against: 11 packs miss: Mexico (LFPDPPP), Vietnam (PDPL), Thailand (PDPA), Indonesia (PDP), Philippines (DPA), Nigeria (NDPA), South Africa (POPIA), Israel (PPL), Argentina (Ley 25.326), Turkey (KVKK), Egypt (PDPL), UK (UK-GDPR post-Brexit). The pack set is Asia-Pacific + Korea-Japan-heavy; LATAM is under-represented; Africa is absent.
hidden_assumptions.validation_strategy: Survey go-to-market plan. Identify top-15 jurisdictions by tenant pipeline. Measure overlap with the 11 packs. If <80%, the pack set is mis-prioritized.
hidden_assumptions.risk_if_wrong: First enterprise tenant in an unrepresented jurisdiction blocks on pack authorship. 6-week unplanned work per pack × N missing jurisdictions.

hidden_assumptions.assumption: Annex III binary gate is sufficient for EU AI Act compliance + future AI regulations
hidden_assumptions.evidence_against: EU AI Act has 4 tiers, not 2. UK AI regulation (forthcoming), US AI EO follow-ups, KR AI Basic Act (2025+), China AI Generative Service measures — all use graduated risk tiers. Binary gate is below the floor of every named regulation.
hidden_assumptions.validation_strategy: Map binary gate to each of 5 named regulations. Identify capabilities where binary gate gives the wrong answer (high-risk in EU, low-risk in KR, or vice versa). Count capabilities where gate misclassifies.
hidden_assumptions.risk_if_wrong: Compliance theater. First EU AI Act audit produces a finding; remediation requires graduated risk classification across all capabilities; M07 retrofit.

hidden_assumptions.assumption: The bc-sources/<bc>/ archive pattern (ADR-0136) is a sustainable preservation mechanism
hidden_assumptions.evidence_against: Archives drift. The ADR creates a new BLOCKER lane (oya-governance-foundry-bc-source-coherence) to enforce coherence between top-level and archive — but lanes catch divergence, they don't prevent it. The archive will either ossify (read-only history) or compete with the top-level (two sources of truth).
hidden_assumptions.validation_strategy: 6-month checkpoint: measure update-frequency of bc-sources/<bc>/ vs top-level foundry/*.md. If archive is updated <10% as often, it's ossified — retire it. If updated >50% as often, it's a competing source — fold it back in.
hidden_assumptions.risk_if_wrong: bc-sources/ becomes zombie code. The PR is conflict-averse compromise architecture: we consolidated AND preserved, getting the costs of both.

hyperscaler_architect_lens_findings.finding: ADR-0136 (Foundry 6→1) conflates product perimeter with service perimeter. AWS Bedrock externally is one API; internally bedrock-runtime, bedrock-agent, bedrock-agent-runtime, bedrock-knowledge-bases are separate SDK clients with separate service teams and separate on-call rotations. The ADR's hyperscaler-shape citation is product-marketing evidence, not service-engineering evidence. Bar Raiser would push back: 'Show me the on-call rotation for each BC. If different, you've just merged their incident perimeters at the wrong layer; if same, you have an org problem your architecture cannot fix.'

ADR-0135 (Connect 8-way split) treats shorts (short-form video) and notes (markdown text) as peer µservices. These have wildly asymmetric operational profiles — shorts needs GPU pools, CDN egress, transcode farms; notes needs CRDT + Postgres. Treating them as peers in a flat topology hides 10× cost asymmetry. Google internally would put shorts under a YouTube-class infra team, not Workspace. The flat topology is conceptually clean but operationally naïve. Also: Workflow + Ontology as the universal inter-µservice adapter is ESB 2.0; Google uses service mesh (Stubby + protobuf), not orchestration, in the data path.

Annex III binary gate is below the floor of every named AI regulation (EU AI Act 4 tiers, KR AI Basic Act tiered, US AI EO follow-ups graduated). 'Annex III: yes/no' is coverage tracking, not risk classification. At first external AI audit, this produces a finding. The hidden assumption: 'AI risk is binary.' AI risk is a continuum across impact-on-rights, deployment-scope, reversibility, opt-model. Also: Loro 1.x bus-factor-1 dependency for 6 µservices is a supply-chain risk that should trigger an explicit bus-factor SLA.

The PR treats ontology as a substrate µservice but doesn't recognize that 3,665 artifact files COULD BE ontology-defined. Each µservice is an instance of an `OntologyMicroservice` type with fields like prd_text, threat_model, slos[]. Render artifacts FROM ontology. Eat your own dogfood. Also: Cedar's schema-bound entity model will fight against ontology's dynamic-type runtime. Cedar fragments are static; ontology types are user-authored. The ADRs don't address this. Recommend Zanzibar-style relationship-based authz overlay for ontology-dynamic types, sitting alongside Cedar for IAM-style policies.

11-pack overlay inheritance model is the model Stripe started with and moved away from. EU vs UK vs Switzerland have 80% overlap with 20% delta — the overlay model duplicates the 80%; constraint composition expresses only the delta. As the pack tree grows (EU → EU-DE → EU-DE-banking), inheritance breaks down. Migrate to constraint composition before the pack tree exceeds 2 levels deep. Also: canonicalizing PRD format is correct; canonicalizing threat-model CONTENT is wrong — verify per-service threat content isn't boilerplate.

The PR ships 1,515 artifacts; the no-silent-regression principle (cited in 7 ADRs) requires that every public contract change carries deprecation notice + version bump + sunset. With 1,515 surfaces, the regression-detection surface is enormous. Where is the inventory of public-contract surfaces protected by no-silent-regression? Without an inventory, the principle is unenforceable. Audit-grade requires the inventory itself be audit-grade.

alternatives_to_reconsider.reconsideration: Rejected reason 'providers are tightly coupled to runtime' is true for synchronous LLM dispatch but false for async pre-warming, embedding generation, and async eval. The 2-way split isolates provider credential blast radius cleanly. Worth reconsidering as a successor ADR after 6 months of foundry-as-one operational data.

None have a first tenant; none have product-market-fit evidence. The 4-way split with deferral matches actual readiness; 'half-measure' label is unfair when half the surfaces are aspirational.

summary: PR #143 ships 1,515 audit-grade artifacts across 17 µservices with strong internal consistency, well-argued ADRs, and a defensible structural shape. The divergent lens surfaces 5 high-probability 12-month regrets and 6 hidden assumptions that the ADRs assert rather than validate. The most consequential: (1) hyperscaler product-surface shape was conflated with hyperscaler service-team shape — foundry consolidation may have copied the marketing diagram, not the architecture; (2) Workflow + Ontology as universal cross-µservice adapter puts orchestration in the data path, a pattern hyperscalers explicitly avoid; (3) Loro 1.x is bus-factor-1 across 6 µservices without a pluggable trait; (4) 11-pack overlay model is the inheritance pattern Stripe moved away from; (5) Annex III binary gate is below the floor of every named AI regulation. Approve with binding follow-up IPs for the 6 highest-leverage mitigations, none of which block PR #143 itself but all of which must complete before M02 promotion. The PR is good; the divergent critique is what makes it better.
